name: Trans-splicing ASO-Mediated Exon Replacement
therapeuticGoalDescription: Replace a defective exon in the endogenous transcript with a wild-type exon delivered via a bifunctional trans-splicing ASO, producing a corrected mRNA that encodes functional protein.
molecularDefect: Loss-of-function mutations located in one or a small number of exons where replacement with wild-type sequence restores a functional protein.
diseaseMechanism: A bifunctional ASO binds both the target pre-mRNA (via antisense to an intronic region flanking the defective exon) and a donor RNA carrying the wild-type exon. The ASO recruits the spliceosome to skip the defective exon and splice in the wild-type donor exon, producing a chimeric mRNA with corrected sequence.
suitableVariantTypes: Exonic point mutations; small insertions/deletions within exons; mutations where replacement of one or a few exons restores reading frame and protein function.
typicalDiseases: Dystrophin restoration in DMD (exon replacement, not skipping); hemoglobinopathies (experimental); other genetic disorders with defined exonic mutations.
rnaTargetRegion: Intronic sequences flanking the target exon on the pre-mRNA; splice donor/acceptor sites of the target exon.
transcriptRequirement: Disease-relevant transcript with a defined exonic mutation amenable to exon replacement. Must have accessible intronic regions for ASO binding.
asoChemistry: Bifunctional ASOs: antisense wing (RNase H-inactive, e.g., PMO or 2'-MOE) for pre-mRNA binding + splice site-blocking wing for spliceosome recruitment.
typicalLength: Antisense wing: 20-30 nt; donor exon construct: variable (typically 100-300 nt including splice signals).
designRules: Identify target exon and flanking intronic sequences; design antisense wing complementary to pre-mRNA intronic region; design donor RNA with wild-type exon + splice signals; validate trans-splicing efficiency by RT-PCR and protein restoration.
secondaryStructureRequirement: Accessible intronic regions for ASO binding; splice signals must be functional on both endogenous pre-mRNA and donor RNA.
offTargetConsiderations: Potential off-target trans-splicing at partially complementary intronic sequences; incomplete replacement may produce chimeric proteins.
advantages: Repairs endogenous transcript without genomic modification; can restore full-length protein from a single exon replacement; leverages natural spliceosome machinery.
limitations: Low trans-splicing efficiency in most systems; bifunctional ASO design is complex; delivery of donor RNA adds complexity; no approved therapies.
clinicalTrialExamples: Preclinical studies in DMD mouse models (exon replacement); no clinical-stage programs.

evidenceLevel.note: Proof-of-concept in animal models; no human clinical data for ASO-mediated trans-splicing.

arbitration.designUnavailableReason: Trans-splicing exon replacement needs a pre-trans-splicing molecule: a binding domain against the target intron, a splice site, and the replacement exon cargo. The binding domain requires intronic sequence and the cargo requires the corrected exon, so this is a distinct construct from anything the current designers build. The mechanism still competes for ranking.
arbitration.flagReason: Preclinical only; trans-splicing efficiency is low and no approved therapy exists. Surfaced qualitatively.
